title: Neurobiology of Chronic Pain, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
authors: Gerald Young; Hella Thielen; Kristin Samuelson; Joel Jin; Ioannis Mavroudis; Dimitrios A. Kazis
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (including chronic low back pain, chronic widespread pain, fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, nociplastic pain), mild traumatic brain injury/concussion, posttraumatic stress disorder
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as a broad heuristic framework to contextualize sensitization mechanisms across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD. It places central/peripheral sensitization within the biological component and notes possible exacerbation from psychological and social factors, but does not operationalize or integrate the three domains substantively.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper asserts that psychological and social factors can exacerbate central/peripheral sensitization, but no pathway or mediator is specified. The fear-avoidance model is applied to MTBI sensory hypersensitivity, but not empirically tested. No triadic mechanism is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper defines BPS as a 'compendium' but also claims it as an explanatory framework, creating a tension between listing and integration
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper asserts that psychological and social factors exacerbate sensitization but provides no mechanism or pathway for this interaction
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper uses the fear-avoidance model for MTBI sensory hypersensitivity but notes it has not been empirically tested in that population
conceptual_tensions_4: The paper proposes a sensitization model as a common mechanism across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD, but the evidence for sensitization in MTBI and PTSD is largely theoretical
additional_observations_1: The paper is primarily a neurobiological review of chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD, with the BPS model used as a broad heuristic framework rather than an operationalized model
additional_observations_2: The paper introduces novel concepts (psychological reserve, psychological control, activation–inhibition coordination) but does not integrate them with the BPS model in a substantive way
additional_observations_3: The paper's sensitization model is the main integrative effort, but it focuses on biological mechanisms and only mentions psychological/social factors as potential exacerbators
additional_observations_4: The paper does not cite Engel (1977/1980) or any foundational BPS source, the model is attributed to Young's own synthesis
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial model as a broad heuristic to contextualize a neurobiological review of sensitization across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD. Biological content is elaborated, psychological content is mentioned, and social content is minimal. The BPS label is used for background framing and as an organizing principle, but no three-domain integration is achieved. The paper defines BPS as a 'compendium' and does not operationalize it.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and no triadic integration is present. Triadic integration is 'none' because the paper only asserts that psychological and social factors can exacerbate biological sensitization without specifying any pathway. Bio-dominant balance reflects the paper's primary focus on neurobiology.

title: Neurobiology of Chronic Pain, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
authors: Gerald Young; Hella Thielen; Kristin Samuelson; Joel Jin; Ioannis Mavroudis; Dimitrios A. Kazis
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain, concussion/mild traumatic brain injury (MTBI), and fear/posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
context_note: Forensic/disability-assessment and court context is emphasized; legal-related and secondary-gain motivations are discussed.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper embeds central/peripheral sensitization in the biological component of BPS and posits psychological reserve/control plus social factors as exacerbations. It uses BPS mainly as a causal scaffold, not as measured variables or a tested three-domain model.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes several top-down/bottom-up pathways: threat appraisal triggers fear and avoidance, which prevents habituation and exacerbates sensory sensitization; GABA–glutamate imbalance increases excitability/arousal/attention, linked to sensory hypersensitivity; pain/fatigue and poor sleep deplete reserve and weaken control. Social/legal factors are described as exacerbating or motivating symptoms, but no full triadic pathway is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS as a broad causal frame but its substantive mechanism is overwhelmingly neurobiological sensitization
conceptual_tensions_2: It generalizes sensitization from chronic pain to MTBI and PTSD while noting direct evidence is limited or lacking
conceptual_tensions_3: It searches for biomarkers but concludes that none are definitive, even while arguing for neurobiological underpinnings
conceptual_tensions_4: The social domain is mostly forensic/legal/secondary-gain content rather than socioeconomic, family, or healthcare-system content
conceptual_tensions_5: The court context treats chronic pain without tissue damage as controversial despite the article's physiological/neurological framing
additional_observations_1: Chronic pain is treated as one component of a broader psychological-injury-and-law frame, alongside MTBI and PTSD
additional_observations_2: The article is a scoping-style literature review of neurobiology rather than a psychosocial intervention review
additional_observations_3: It names several instruments and diagnostic systems, but they are used conceptually or as cited measures rather than pooled in a meta-analysis
additional_observations_4: The paper's integration is strongest at neural and cognitive-behavioral levels and thinnest at the social level
additional_observations_5: The BPS label does explanatory and therapeutic work, but the paper does not operationalize BPS as measured variables or formal constructs
additional_observations_6: The paper repeatedly distinguishes biological mechanisms from forensic/legal interpretations of psychological injury
synthesis_note: The article uses BPS mainly as a causal scaffold around neurobiological sensitization. Biological content is developed; psychological concepts are linked through reserve/control, fear-avoidance, and attention networks; social content is mostly forensic/legal. It proposes some top-down/bottom-up pathways but not a full three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant pseudo-BPS: all domains appear, but social/legal factors are thin and triadic reasoning remains partial.

title: Neurobiology of Chronic Pain, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
authors: Gerald Young; Hella Thielen; Kristin Samuelson; Joel Jin; Ioannis Mavroudis; Dimitrios A. Kazis
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain, mild traumatic brain injury, posttraumatic stress disorder
context_note: Forensic context involving motor vehicle accidents and tort litigation
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes the review into three psychological injury conditions (chronic pain, MTBI, PTSD) and discusses sensitization mechanisms across them, positioning BPS as a broad causal framework rather than an integrated model.
integration_mechanism_summary: Proposes that sensitization processes (central, peripheral, sensory, perceptual) operate across biological and psychological domains, with fear and avoidance behaviors exacerbating sensitization. No social domain integration proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS as a heuristic compendium versus an integrated explanatory framework
conceptual_tensions_2: Absence of definitive biomarkers despite extensive neurobiological discussion
conceptual_tensions_3: Minimal social domain coverage despite BPS framing
conceptual_tensions_4: Forensic context introduces legal/social factors that may not integrate with biological/psychological mechanisms
additional_observations_1: The review focuses on three related psychological injuries (chronic pain, MTBI, PTSD) rather than a single pain condition
additional_observations_2: Sensitization is proposed as a unifying mechanism across all three conditions
additional_observations_3: The review explicitly positions itself in a forensic/legal context with implications for disability assessment and tort litigation
additional_observations_4: Psychological concepts are primarily discussed in relation to fear-avoidance and cognitive processing rather than comprehensive psychological constructs
synthesis_note: This scoping review examines neurobiological mechanisms across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD, using the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework. It elaborates biological content (sensitization mechanisms, neuroimaging findings, neurotransmitter imbalances) and mentions psychological constructs (fear, anxiety, cognitive processing) but provides minimal social domain coverage. The BPS model functions as a heuristic compendium rather than an integrated explanatory framework, with integration primarily between biological and psychological domains through sensitization mechanisms. The review's forensic context introduces legal/social factors as contextual rather than integrated components.
coding_rationale: BPS typology as 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but social domain is minimal. Triadic integration as 'none' because social domain lacks integration with biological and psychological domains. Bio-dominant balance due to extensive neurobiological content versus minimal social coverage.
